unit.title: The biases that cost you money
unit.description: The mental shortcuts that make you buy high, sell low and think you're a genius

u27l1.title: Your brain isn't built for investing

texts: Two and a half years on a rollercoaster
January 2024: spot bitcoin ETFs launch in the US. You put **€10,000** into bitcoin and watch it week by week, with real data. You can sell whenever you like.
Go all the way to the end, whether you sell or not.

Buying after rises and selling after falls creates the **investor gap**. In spot bitcoin ETFs, between January 2024 and June 2026, investors got **−5.8 %** a year versus **+8.5 %** for the ETF itself.
You've sold. Was that your plan deciding, or your gut?
Way above what you put in! Your brain is screaming: «Put more in!».
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
Who's deciding?
Daniel Kahneman, Nobel Prize in Economics: we have a **system 1**, fast and emotional, and a **system 2**, slow and analytical. Which one is deciding?
System 1: fast and emotional
System 2: slow and analytical
Selling everything after reading a scary headline
Fear and haste: system 1 in charge.
Working out your system's expectancy from your journal
Doing the maths calmly is system 2's job.
Buying because everyone's talking about it
Following the crowd is a quick system 1 shortcut.
Rereading your plan before trading
A written checklist forces you to think slowly.
Dodging a scooter coming straight at you
Here system 1 saves you: it's fast and automatic.
Sort the five decisions.
System 1 is perfect for dodging a car. For investing, **force yourself to use system 2**: fear, haste and euphoria make bad decisions.
Hint: is there emotion and haste, or calm and numbers?
System 1 or system 2? Sort each decision

steps.title: The investor gap
steps.body:
Morningstar, 10 years to 2025: US funds returned **9.9 %** a year; their investors' money, flowing in and out, returned **8.7 %**: 1.2 points less a year.

In the most volatile funds, the gap was −2.1 points; in the calm ones, −0.4.
steps.key: The product may be good; the problem is behaviour: buying after rises and selling after falls.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi, in My biases mode, to review your last trade.

texts: Heads or tails with Dani
Dani
Here's a game: I toss a coin.
If it's heads, I give you **€150**. If it's tails, you give me **€100**.
Are you in?
No: losing €100 would hurt too much
That's what almost everyone does… even though on average you'd win €25.
Yes: on average I win €25 per toss
Only if I toss the coin
The coin is fair: the problem is in our heads.
Kahneman and Tversky (1979): losing hurts **twice as much** as winning feels good.
That's why we turn down bets that are good for us.
And if you play lots of times
1,000 people take Dani's game: heads **+€150**, tails **−€100**. What happens if they keep playing?
If each one plays 100 times, how many end up losing?
Half, same as with one toss
Hardly anyone
Almost everyone
Only **2 %** end up losing, and on average they win about €2,488. With positive expectancy, repeating works in your favour.
Raise the tosses until 5 in 100 or fewer lose.
**Loss aversion** makes us turn down decisions that are good for us. And watching every toss, or your portfolio every day, makes you see more losses: that's **myopic loss aversion**.
Hardly anyone loses! Turning it down out of fear was costly.
With a single toss, half lose: that's what's scary.
Raise how many times each person plays

steps.title: How to protect yourself
steps.body:
When we're losing, we get **riskier** («I'll double up to win it back»); when we're winning, **more cautious**.

Set your stop before you get in, while you're calm. And ask yourself the right question: not «how much have I lost?», but **«if I didn't own it, would I buy it today at this price?»**.
steps.key: Losing hurts twice as much as winning feels good: that's why we cling on to losers.
steps.tip: Try it: look at the reddest position in your Portfolio: would you buy it today?

texts: Laura needs €2,000
Laura
I need €2,000 and I own two stocks.
A is at **+20 %**. B is at **−20 %** and has just reported bad results.
Which one should she sell?
A, which is in the green
That's the **disposition effect**: selling the one doing well and keeping the one getting worse.
Whichever has the worse outlook, green or red
That's it! If B has got worse and A hasn't, maybe it's time to sell B.
Both, and stop investing
Running away from everything doesn't fix the bias: it just swaps it for another.
Odean (1998): the winners that were sold went on to perform **better** than the losers that were kept.
Let your profits run
Real candles. This trader puts the stop far away and the target very close: cutting profits short and letting losses run. Fix it.
You're right 60 % of the time, but you close wins at +0.5R and let losses run to −2R. Do you make or lose money?
Make: you're right more than half the time
Lose: each miss wipes out four wins
Break even
0.6 × 0.5 − 0.4 × 2 = **−0.5R** per trade. The disposition effect sinks a good win rate.
Put the target at least twice as far away as the stop and see what happened.
**Cut your losses and let your profits run**: the exit is decided before you get in, not when you see the first bit of green.
Target hit! You let the profit run.
The stop was hit: a loss decided in advance. That's how you cut it.
Your target is closer than your stop: you win little when you're right.
Place the stop and the target, and see what happened

steps.title: How to protect yourself
steps.body: Stop and exit plan **before** you get in. If the trade goes your way, the plan decides the exit (for example, half at 2R and the rest with a trailing stop), not the fear of giving back what you've made.
steps.key: We sell winners for a quick buzz and hold losers so we don't have to admit a mistake.
steps.tip: Try it: on your next buy, set the target twice as far away as the stop.

texts: Got a good eye?
Four real charts, with no name or date. Up or down? Keep count of how many you get right.
Play all four rounds.
With 4 tries, getting them all right by chance happens **more than once in twenty**. To know if you have an edge you need **lots of logged trades**.
Three right… feeling like a genius already? Careful.
Done. With 4 tries, your score says next to nothing.
One hit or miss on its own means nothing. Keep going.
Look at the chart: up or down?
The one who trades most
Marcos
Carla
I've made 40 trades this month. I know the market inside out.
I've made 2. The rest is my automatic contribution.
In the long run, who usually earns more?
Marcos: the more he trades, the more he earns
Barber and Odean (2000): the households that traded most earned **11.4 %** a year.
Carla: trading a lot tends to be costly
That's it! The heaviest traders: **11.4 %** a year. The market: **17.9 %**.
Same: it all comes down to luck
No: the heaviest traders earned 11.4 %; the market, 17.9 %.
The main cause: **overconfidence**. We think we know more than we do.

steps.title: Luck or skill
steps.body:
A few early wins are the most dangerous thing for a beginner: they **mistake luck for skill**, raise their risk and break their own rules.

Among lots of people, there will always be some «geniuses» by pure luck.
steps.key: Getting it right two or three times doesn't make you an expert: with few trades, luck is in charge.
steps.tip: Try it: compare your Portfolio with the S&P 500 ETF since your first buy.

texts: Until he gets his €40 back
Pablo
I bought at **€40**. After some bad results, it's now worth **€25**.
I'm not selling until I'm back at €40. I've already lost too much.
What's happening to Pablo?
Nothing: the price will come back
It may or may not. The €40 only matters to him, not to the market.
He's anchored to his purchase price
Exactly! It's **anchoring**, with a bit of sunk cost and loss aversion.
He should buy more to bring down his average price
Averaging down because of an anchor means putting in more money without reviewing the business.
The question: with €25 in cash, would he buy this share today, knowing what he knows?
Honestly… no.
Which bias is talking?
Each sentence sounds reasonable… until you see the bias behind it. Which one is it?
Anchoring
Sunk cost
Confirmation
«It was at €120; at €70 it's a steal»
The €120 is an anchor: it says nothing about today's value.
«I've already lost €3,000, I can't sell now»
What's lost doesn't come back by holding on: decide from today.
«I only follow people who think like me»
That way you won't see the warning signs when they come.
«It's down 50 %: it's half price»
It may have fallen because the business is worth half… or less.
«I've put so much into it that I'm not giving up now»
The time and money already spent don't change what makes sense today.
«I mute anyone who criticises the company»
You only read what agrees with you: that's confirmation.
Label the six sentences.
The past price says nothing about value, **what's lost doesn't come back** and people agreeing with you doesn't make you right. Antidote: write down **three reasons you could be wrong**.
Hint: is it looking at a price, at what's already lost, or only at like-minded opinions?
Anchoring, sunk cost or confirmation?

steps.title: Your takeaway
steps.body: Value things with today's data (earnings, debt, business), not with the price you paid or the price it used to be. And deliberately look for the **opposite view**.
steps.key: Falling a lot doesn't make something cheap. People agreeing with you doesn't make you right.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi for three reasons against your next buy.

texts: Live through 1929
January 1929. The US stock market has been rising for years and «everyone» is buying. You put **€10,000** into the S&P 500, with real data.
Go all the way to the end, whether you sell or not.
From the September 1929 peak it fell **86 %** and didn't get back there until 1954, not counting dividends. **What just happened doesn't predict what's next**: look at decades of data, not months.
You've sold. See how long it took to come back…
More than half gone. And in 1929 everyone thought it would keep rising.
It just keeps going up. Will it always be like this?
Hit start. You can sell whenever you like
Ten get-rich stories
Iván
Look: ten people who got rich with a small crypto.
If they could, so can I.
Which conclusion is right?
It's a sure way to get rich
You only see the ones who won. The thousands who lost don't post about it.
I can't see the ones who did the same and lost everything
That's **survivorship bias**! And in crypto you can lose everything you put in.
The best thing is to copy whoever made the most
You're copying a survivor without knowing how many fell along the way.
A fact from Bessembinder, using US shares since 1926:
Just **4 %** of them accounted for the market's entire net gain.
And **more than half** returned less than Treasury bills.

steps.title: What you take away
steps.body:
**Recency** makes whatever just happened weigh too much: after a rise, «it always goes up»; after a fall, «it can only go down». **Survivorship** only shows you the ones who won.

The antidote: decades of data and the whole market, not the cases that show up on social media.
steps.key: Neither last year nor the visible winners tell the whole story.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open the S&P 500 ETF and look for its past falls.

u27l1-1.prompt: According to Morningstar, how much less a year did the average investor earn than their own funds over the 10 years to 2025?
options: Nothing
Around 1.2 points
About 10 points
u27l1-1.explanation: 9.9 % for the funds versus 8.7 % for their investors, from buying and selling at the wrong time.

u27l1-5.prompt: One Monday you read: «Stock markets plunge 4 %». You have an index fund for 20 years from now and your heart is racing. What do you do?
options: Buy loads more with my whole emergency fund
Sell now, before it falls further
Take a breath, reread my plan and touch nothing today
u27l1-5.explanation: Big decisions should never be made with your heart racing.
feedback: Reacting with your emergency fund is also deciding in the heat of the moment.
That's system 1 in charge. This is how the investor gap is made: selling after the fall.
Good: you're giving system 2 time. One bad day doesn't change a 20-year plan.

u27l1-6.prompt: In spot bitcoin ETFs, what did investors get compared with the ETF itself?
options: Exactly the same
Quite a bit more than the ETF
Much less: around −5.8 % versus +8.5 %
u27l1-6.explanation: They bought at the peaks and sold in the dips. These are annual returns between January 2024 and June 2026.

u27l1-8.prompt: What tends to put system 1 in charge? Select all that apply.
options: Being in a hurry
Euphoria
A written checklist
Fear
u27l1-8.explanation: A written checklist forces you to think slowly: it's a system 2 tool.

u27l1-9.prompt: The problem behind the gap isn't the product, it's the investor's ____.
options: broker
country
salary
behaviour
u27l1-9.explanation: The same fund gives different results depending on how you get in and out.

u27l1-10.prompt: What do you explain to Lumi?
options: You probably got in and out at the wrong time: that's the investor gap
It's definitely a scam
Funds always lie in their figures
u27l1-10.explanation: Your return depends on the fund and on when you get in and out.
feedback: Oops… I bought when it was at its highs and sold in the March scare. Touché.
Maybe not: if you got in after the rises and out in the falls, the difference is down to you.
The fund's performance figures are real; what changes is when you were invested.
lines: My fund has made 10 % a year… but I've made way less! 🤨

u27l2-1.prompt: According to prospect theory, a loss of €100 hurts roughly…
options: As much as winning €100 feels good
Half as much
Twice as much as winning €100 feels good

u27l2-4.prompt: If a loss hurts twice as much as a gain of the same size, how much would you need to win to emotionally make up for a loss of €100?
u27l2-4.explanation: €100 × 2 = €200: that's why many people only accept bets where the gain is double.

u27l2-6.prompt: Marta has a share that's down 30 %. The company has cut its forecasts and lost its biggest customer. She says: «I'm not selling until I'm back to even». What question should she ask herself?
options: What are they saying on the forum?
If I didn't own it, would I buy it today at this price, knowing what I know?
How much have I lost already?
u27l2-6.explanation: The right decision looks at the business's future, not at your purchase price.
feedback: Looking for encouragement doesn't change the company's business.
Good: that way she decides with today's information, not her purchase price.
Focusing on what's been lost only feeds loss aversion.

u27l2-8.prompt: The key question: «If I didn't own it, would I ____ it today at this price?».
options: sell
forget
give away
buy
u27l2-8.explanation: It separates the decision from your purchase price.

options: I'm out because the stop I set earlier was hit
I turn down a bet with positive expected value because I'm scared of losing
I double my position to win it back sooner
I won't sell until I get back what I paid
I sell because the business has got worse
u27l2-9.explanation: Sound decisions look at the plan and the business; the others look at the pain of losing.

u27l2-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Being wrong is normal; what matters is deciding with what you know today
Buy more to bring your average price down
Well done, hold on until it comes back
u27l2-10.explanation: Accepting a small loss in time is part of the game, not a failure.
feedback: You're right: the market doesn't know what I paid. I'll review the business, not my pride.
Averaging down without reviewing the business is putting more money into the same mistake.
Sometimes it doesn't come back. And while you wait, that money could be somewhere better.
lines: I'm not selling that share at a loss 😤
Selling would mean admitting I got it wrong.

options: Spreading your money across lots of assets
Selling winners too early and holding losers too long
Always buying whatever is rising most
u27l3-1.explanation: Odean measured it in 1998 across thousands of accounts.

u27l3-2.prompt: You buy at the last price with a €10,000 account and a maximum risk of 1 %. Set your stop now, calmly, before the price moves.
u27l3-2.explanation: Setting the stop before you get in stops loss aversion from convincing you to hold on «until it comes back» if the price falls.

u27l3-7.prompt: Disposition effect or following the plan?
options: Removing the stop because «it's nearly there»
Selling half at 2R, as the plan says
Exiting because the stop set before entry was hit
Selling at +5 % for fear of losing it
Holding a share at −40 % «until it comes back»
u27l3-7.explanation: The difference is who's deciding: the plan written calmly or the emotion of the moment.

u27l3-8.prompt: The classic advice: cut your losses and let your ____ run.
options: fees
news
losses
profits
u27l3-8.explanation: The disposition effect does the exact opposite.

options: Yes, lock it in, you never know
What did your exit plan say before you got in?
Buy more with everything you've got
u27l3-10.explanation: The exit is decided before you get in, not when you see the first bit of green.
feedback: It might work out today, but if you always do it, you cut short your best trades.
Hmm… It said half at 2R and the rest with a trailing stop. OK, I'll stick to the plan.
Swinging from fear to euphoria in a minute isn't a plan either.
lines: I'll sell it now, before it drops.

u27l5-7.prompt: Quick: according to Barber and Odean (2001), how much more did men trade than women?
options: Half as much
The same
45 % more
u27l5-7.explanation: And their net returns fell by more than women's.

u27l5-8.prompt: Winning your first trades proves you have skill.
options: True
False
u27l5-8.explanation: With only a few trades, luck counts for a huge amount. It's exactly when the danger of raising your risk is greatest.

u27l5-9.prompt: Bruno has got 3 trades in a row right in the simulator. He wants to triple his size «because he's got the hang of it now». What's going on?
options: Overconfidence: he should keep the same risk and keep recording
He should stop using stops
Nothing, three in a row prove he knows what he's doing
u27l5-9.explanation: After several wins, the rule stays the same: the risk per trade doesn't change.
feedback: Good: your risk per trade doesn't change because you're on a winning run.
Winning streaks don't remove the risk; they only hide it.
Three in a row by chance happens one time in eight. It proves nothing.

u27l5-10.prompt: What protects you from overconfidence? Select all that apply.
options: Writing down three reasons you could be wrong
Raising your risk after every win
Comparing yourself with an index over several years
Tracking your results in a journal
u27l5-10.explanation: Raising your risk after a win is exactly what overconfidence does.

u27l5-11.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Then raise the risk on your next buys
With four tries, luck rules: you need many more recorded trades
Yes: four out of four is no coincidence
u27l5-11.explanation: With few tries, luck looks a lot like talent: only a large, measured sample tells them apart. The temptation is to believe a four-round scoreboard.
feedback: Raising the risk after a short streak is textbook overconfidence.
OK: I'll note it down and keep measuring. We'll see what my score says after many more.
By chance, getting all four right happens more than once in twenty. It may well be.
lines: I got all four rounds of «up or down?» right.
I think I have a gift for this.

options: Making 40 trades a month because «I know the market by heart»
Trusting your memory to know how you're doing
Comparing your result with an index over several years
Raising the risk after three wins in a row
Keeping the same risk after a good streak
u27l5-12.explanation: Prudence measures and sticks to the rules; overconfidence changes them as soon as a few wins come along. And memory keeps the wins and forgets the mistakes.

u27l6-2.prompt: Match each bias with its antidote.
options: Anchoring
Sunk cost
Confirmation
Gambler's fallacy
u27l6-2.explanation: Every mental shortcut has a question that takes it apart.
right: Decide from today, ignoring what's been lost
Remember that each day is almost independent

u27l6-5.prompt: Ana has bought a share. Since then she only reads bullish forums and mutes anyone who criticises the company. What habit would you recommend?
options: Write down three reasons she could be wrong and read opposing views
Sell immediately
Carry on like this, it's good vibes
u27l6-5.explanation: You fight confirmation bias by deliberately looking for what contradicts you.
feedback: Good: if her reasons stand up to the criticism, great. If not, better to know now.
She doesn't need to sell: she needs to look at the other side.
Good vibes and bad decisions: she won't see the warning signs.

u27l6-8.prompt: Before buying, write down three reasons you could be ____.
options: right
calm
winning
wrong
u27l6-8.explanation: It's the simplest antidote to confirmation bias.

u27l6-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Cheap or expensive depends on what the business is worth, not on where the price used to be
Yes, half price is always a bargain
Wait for it to drop another 50 % and it'll be even cheaper
u27l6-10.explanation: Stock market sales aren't like supermarket sales: the product may have changed too.
feedback: True. First I'll look at earnings, debt and why it fell. The old price isn't a price tag.
Not in the stock market: it may have fallen because the business is worth half… or less.
That's still only looking at the price, not the value.
lines: It's half price, like in the sales!

u27l7-1.prompt: Look at just these two months of a real chart. What trend do you see? (Visa · closes every 3 sessions · September–November 2026)
options: Uptrend
Downtrend
Sideways
u27l7-1.explanation: It's clearly rising. Recency makes us believe it will always carry on like this; a two-month stretch says nothing about the coming years.

u27l7-2.prompt: This is how Japan's Nikkei was doing up to December 1989. Tap the highest point. (Nikkei 225 · monthly closes · up to December 1989)
u27l7-2.explanation: After years of rises, everyone thought it would carry on. The late-1989 peak took 34 years to get back to.

u27l7-4.prompt: After two years of strong rises, Laura believes the market «always goes up» and puts all her savings in. Which bias is she mainly showing?
options: Sunk cost
Loss aversion
Recency
u27l7-4.explanation: She's giving too much weight to what has just happened (and there's probably some overconfidence too).

u27l7-7.prompt: After a 30 % fall, Marta is convinced the market «can only go down now» and wants to sell her long-term index fund. What would you tell her?
options: To look at decades of data and reread her plan before deciding
To wait for it to rise 30 % before buying back in
She's right: what falls keeps falling
u27l7-7.explanation: Whatever happened last weighs too heavily in our heads: long-run data balances it out.
feedback: Good: the long-run history includes lots of falls followed by recoveries.
Selling low and buying back high is the most expensive way to invest.
That's recency in reverse. The big falls of 2009 and 2020 were followed by strong recoveries.

u27l7-9.prompt: Where can survivorship bias be hiding? Select all that apply.
options: Influencers who only show their wins
An index that includes every company in the market
Testing a system only on companies that exist today
Fund rankings that leave out the ones that closed
u27l7-9.explanation: A broad index doesn't pick winners after the fact: it buys the whole market.

options: «Look how many people have got rich from this»
«After this fall, it can only go down now»
«This fund manager's funds always win» (the bad ones have already closed)
«The market has gone up for two years: it always goes up»
u27l7-10.explanation: Recency: the recent past weighs too much. Survivorship: you only see the ones still standing.

u27l6-11.prompt: An analyst publishes that a certain share «is worth €200». Weeks later, with worse results, you're still thinking about that €200. What's happening to you?
options: I've anchored on the first figure I saw
I have confirmation bias
Nothing: €200 is its value
feedback: That's it: the anchor can be your purchase price, a high or someone else's figure.
That would be looking only for what proves you right. Here the problem is clinging to a number.
It was an estimate made with other data. If the data change, so does the figure.
u27l6-11.explanation: Any number can act as an anchor. Value it again with today's data.
